#5098. XRP Hit 29 Cents in Kraken’s Canadian Market Sell-Off

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP Hit 29 Cents in Kraken’s Canadian Market Sell-Off

XRP traded at just 29 cents in Kraken’s Canadian-dollar market during a localized sell-off, raising questions about thin liquidity.

XRP reportedly traded at just 29 cents in Kraken’s Canadian-dollar market during a sharp, localized sell-off discussed by crypto commentator Crypto Sensei.

His video examines whether the trades reflected an exchange-specific liquidity problem rather than a broader XRP collapse, alongside falling ledger activity and disputed price forecasts.

According to the account presented in the video, 11 Canadian-dollar markets fell by at least 65%, with bitcoin trading below 18,000 and ether around 560.

The host cites November 20, 2026 as the incident date and reports that Kraken considered the orders correctly processed and would let the trades stand.

The analyst didn’t include trade records or Kraken’s full statement. Those limits matter: the reported 29-cent execution should not be confused with XRP’s prevailing price across exchanges.

Crypto Sensei attributes the dislocation to heavy selling meeting insufficient liquidity. Buyers may have secured steep discounts, while sellers received prices far below those available elsewhere.

“Whoever sold and just got totally wiped out here, I feel for you,” he says. The video does not establish whether individual losses resulted from discretionary sales, automated orders or liquidations.

A separate headline claiming the XRP Ledger had lost 60% of its users also draws scrutiny.

The underlying figure, according to the clarification cited in the YouTube video, was roughly a 63% decline in daily activity, not evidence that a comparable share of holders permanently departed or sold their XRP.

The host challenges Jake Claver’s repeated $100 year-end XRP forecast, arguing that institutional adoption is a longer process than such targets suggest. He also distinguishes Ripple’s business expansion from confirmed institutional use of XRP itself.

Former Ripple executive and Evernorth CEO Ashish Birla offers a longer-term XRP development case in a clip: Evernorth intends to deploy XRP on-chain, pursue yield and support ecosystem features rather than simply hold the asset. The video leaves the execution details and eventual returns unresolved.

For HODLers, these are separate questions: whether an exchange has enough liquidity, whether ledger usage is growing, and whether adoption creates demand for XRP. A dramatic trade print, or an ambitious treasury strategy, does not answer all three.

#5097. Tether Gold Under Pressure: Bitcoin and Gold Losses Erase 70% of USDT’s Cushion

Falling gold and Bitcoin prices erase an estimated $5.7 billion from Tether’s holdings, putting its USDT reserve cushion under pressure.

Gold just slid toward $3,500 an ounce and silver fell below $40, extending a sell-off that has put Tether gold back in focus. Why? Tether keeps billions of dollars of gold bars in the reserves behind USDT, so the crash hits its balance sheet directly.

Based on Tether’s latest reserves report and the blockchain, the company holds about 168 tons of gold: 142.8 tons it owns in its USDT reserves, plus 25.7 tons backing its Tether Gold (XAUT) token.

Gold just crashed below $3,500 and silver below $40, hitting their lowest levels in almost 15 months.

$1.2 TRILLION has been wiped out from gold and silver in the last 24 hours. pic.twitter.com/7OLr78DM1N

— Bull Theory (@BullTheoryio) November 25, 2026

At today’s prices, the gold Tether owns has lost about $3.2 billion of value since September 30. Add Bitcoin’s slide, and about 70% of Tether’s $7.95 billion reserve cushion is gone on paper.

USDT, meanwhile, is shrinking. Its supply has fallen $16 billion from its May peak.

The sell-off has picked up speed over the past two weeks:

Higher rates hurt gold because it pays no interest.

The XAUT gold belongs to token holders, so its price swings hit them. The 142.8 tons in the reserves are Tether’s own, so their losses come out of Tether’s cushion.

Tether’s assets topped its liabilities by $7.95 billion on September 30. That gap is the cushion that protects USDT holders if Tether’s investments lose value.

We repriced Tether’s two riskiest holdings at Wednesday’s prices.

That is not the full picture. Tether earns interest on $122.8 billion of US Treasury bills, and it reported profits of $1.04 billion and $1.5 billion in the first two quarters of 2026. Fourth-quarter income will rebuild part of the gap. Its $4.18 billion of stocks, which the report says include gold and bitcoin exposure, may have fallen too.

Tether’s main business is also cooling. USDT supply peaked at $190.4 billion on May 20. It stood at $174.4 billion on Wednesday.

Redemptions shrink the pile of Treasury bills that earns Tether’s interest income. Falling rates would hurt too, but for now the market expects the Fed to raise them.

XAUT trades at $3,473. Our chart uses PAX Gold (PAXG), a rival token that also tracks one ounce of gold, because its Binance history goes back much further than XAUT’s March listing.

PAXG trades at $3,478, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $3,924, and its 200-day EMA at $4,187.

Tether gold is still a huge pile of metal, and Tether earned more than $1 billion in each of the first two quarters. But its reserve cushion now depends on gold and bitcoin stopping their fall.

#5096. LINK, AAVE and UNI Now Supported by Fidelity

Fidelity Investments now supports three new cryptocurrencies on its retail crypto trading platform: Chainlink (LINK), Aave (AAVE) and Uniswap (UNI).

The firm expanded from five available cryptocurrencies to eight on Nov. 24. In just one day, Fidelity added the same number of digital assets that it had added in the four years since it first made Bitcoin and Ether available for customer trading.

Eligible U.S. customers can trade these three tokens on the Fidelity website and app. Some states may have limited access to Fidelity's services.

Fidelity's three new listings include tokens that represent different areas of decentralized finance. Aave is a lending protocol where users can deposit crypto assets to earn interest or use them as collateral for loans. AAVE token holders can vote on changes to the protocol's lending markets and other aspects of its operation.

Uniswap is a decentralized trading platform where users can trade different tokens using shared pools of assets provided by other users. UNI is the Uniswap governance token.

Chainlink provides the data that blockchain apps need to operate. For example, a lending protocol might use a Chainlink price feed to assess the value of collateral for a borrower's loan. Chainlink (LINK) tokens are used to pay for services provided on its network.

Fidelity Crypto started accepting customers from its waitlist in November 2022. At the time, the only two cryptocurrencies it offered were Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH). By March 2023, Fidelity was offering its service to more eligible U.S. investors, but these were still the only cryptocurrencies it allowed customers to trade.

On July 17, 2024, Fidelity added Litecoin (LTC) to its list of cryptocurrencies, bringing the total to three. Over a year later, on Oct. 23, 2025, the company introduced Solana (SOL). In addition to individual retail accounts, Solana became available for crypto IRAs, wealth managers and institutional clients.

Fidelity added its fifth cryptocurrency on Feb. 4, 2026, when it launched Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD) as its first stablecoin available to retail and institutional investors. Eligible users can exchange or redeem each FIDD token for $1. Fidelity waives its usual crypto trading fee when users exchange FIDD for dollars.

In short, the past 24 hours have been a textbook example of extreme market volatility.

Bitcoin failed to hold its post-NVDA rally, showing that buyers remain cautious.

Whale activity and the $55k supply cluster point to more downside risk before a recovery.

#5094. Solana Price Prediction 2030: Is $2,000 SOL Still on the Table After a 75% Crash?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Solana has lost roughly 75% of its value since reaching an all-time high of $294 in January 2025. Large futures traders are leaning bearish, yet institutional analysts continue to see a future in which SOL trades at four digit prices. So, how realistic is a $2,000 Solana price prediction for 2030?

At around $73, SOL is trading at a fraction of the price some of Wall Street’s most optimistic forecasts suggest it could eventually reach. But a steep discount to an analyst’s target does not necessarily make an asset cheap.

NewsBTC examined liquidation heatmaps, whale positions, historical price action, network economics and institutional valuation models to understand where Solana stands today and what it could realistically be worth by the end of the decade.

The findings paint a more complicated picture than either bulls or bears might expect.

Perhaps the most interesting signal right now comes from the derivatives market.

According to a November 23 snapshot from PumpGlass, only around 20% of the tracked Binance whale position value was allocated to longs. Meanwhile, approximately 79% of the broader trader accounts were positioned long.

Although the two figures measure different aspects of market positioning, the divergence is striking. Large traders appear considerably less optimistic than the wider trading crowd.

The average entry price of tracked whale shorts stood near $77.63, compared with $77.05 for whale longs. With SOL trading around $73 at the time of observation, the short side was better positioned.

The on-chain picture offers another reason for caution.

On November 19, blockchain tracker Lookonchain reported that two large holders had unstaked a combined 2.31 million SOL worth approximately $169.4 million before transferring the tokens to Coinbase Prime-associated addresses.

Exchange deposits do not necessarily mean those tokens were sold. Institutional investors use custody platforms for several purposes, including collateral management and portfolio rebalancing. Still, the movement is worth monitoring.

What matters now is whether large holders begin accumulating again or whether the recent decline has further to run.

Solana’s liquidation heatmap reveals an interesting battle developing around its current trading range.

PumpGlass identified several concentrations of potentially vulnerable leveraged positions in its November 23, 19:22 UTC observation.

A recovery toward $79 could put considerable pressure on short sellers. Conversely, a breakdown below $69 could expose another wave of leveraged longs to forced closures.

Data from CoinGlass adds another layer to the picture. At 21:31 UTC on November 23, Solana’s futures open interest stood at $3.86 billion, while rolling 24-hour liquidations reached approximately $30.59 million. Shorts accounted for roughly 72% of those liquidations.

SOL had gained around 3.1% over the same rolling period.

The recovery is consistent with some bearish positions being forced out of the market. However, a liquidated short is not the same as a new investor buying SOL for the next four years.

Until stronger spot demand emerges, traders should be careful about interpreting a short squeeze as the beginning of a sustainable recovery.

Liquidation concentrations are modeled estimates, not guaranteed future orders, and can change considerably as traders adjust their positions.

Solana’s price structure has deteriorated considerably since its September recovery.

After closing July near $72.79, SOL climbed to $103 in August and $117.99 in September. The recovery subsequently unraveled, with October closing near $95.35 before prices returned to the low $70s in November.

Looking at SOL’s historical price action on Binance, using the TradingView SOLUSDT market as the chart reference, five key price regions stand out:

The daily Relative Strength Index was in the low 30s in the observed CoinGlass data, suggesting weak momentum and proximity to oversold territory.

But oversold markets can remain oversold.

A sustained recovery above $80 would be the first encouraging development. Reclaiming $95 and subsequently $100 would provide stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control.

On the downside, failure to hold the $65 range would bring Solana’s 2026 low near $60.42 back into focus.

Our technical assessment remains cautious. There is room for a meaningful relief rally, particularly given the nearby short-liquidation exposure, but the broader market structure has yet to establish a convincing reversal.

While Solana’s price has struggled, its blockchain continues to facilitate substantial financial activity.

According to DefiLlama, Solana’s November 23 network metrics included:

There is something particularly interesting about those last two figures.

Applications running on Solana generated considerably more revenue than the chain itself under DefiLlama’s respective measurement definitions.

This highlights what could become Solana’s biggest valuation challenge.

A blockchain can attract substantial activity and billions of dollars in trading volume without its native token capturing a proportional share of that economic value.

Cheap transactions are excellent for adoption. Whether they are equally good for SOL’s valuation is another question entirely.

That is why Solana’s expansion beyond speculative trading could prove so important.

The blockchain’s growing presence in stablecoins, payments and tokenized real-world assets opens the door to financial activity that could persist even when speculative markets cool.

Its infrastructure is also evolving. The Solana Foundation reported the activation of Alpenglow in October 2026, targeting transaction finality near 150 milliseconds. November’s introduction of Solana 1.0 marked another milestone in the network’s development.

Meanwhile, the announced integration with DTCC’s Tokenization Service, expected in the second half of 2027, could represent a meaningful institutional opportunity.

The real test will be how much financial activity these developments ultimately bring onchain, and how much value SOL captures from it.

Institutional research offers a glimpse into how differently analysts view Solana’s future.

VanEck’s October 2023 research produced one of the widest forecast ranges, with its most optimistic scenario placing SOL above $3,200.

Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick was reported in February 2026 to have projected a $2,000 Solana price by 2030, partly based on the network’s potential in stablecoin micropayments.

However, the bank’s reported $250 end-of-2026 target looks increasingly difficult to achieve from current levels. Its original research note was not available for independent review.

Perhaps the most interesting analysis comes from Bitwise’s November 2026 research, which connects Solana’s future valuation to tokenized stock trading.

The asset manager’s base case assumes Solana captures 50% of tokenized-stock trading volume in 2031, generating approximately $6.75 billion in annual network economic value.

Applying a 40-times valuation multiple produces an estimated SOL price of $385, based on a projected total supply of 700 million tokens.

The report acknowledges the key dependency:

Most of the price increase depends on how quickly stocks move onchain.

In its bullish scenario, Solana captures 65% of tokenized-stock trading, generating approximately $12.83 billion in network economic value and supporting a modeled price of $1,100.

These assumptions reveal just how much needs to go right before four-digit SOL prices become fundamentally convincing.

Here is something many price predictions overlook: Solana’s token supply will not necessarily remain where it is today.

Unlike Bitcoin, SOL has no fixed maximum supply. Its inflationary issuance framework rewards validators and staking participants, while future governance decisions can influence the rate of supply growth.

With around 592 million SOL currently circulating, we use an illustrative assumption of 690 million total tokens by 2030 for our valuation scenarios.

The numbers put popular price targets into perspective.

These are total-supply valuations rather than projected circulating market capitalizations.

At $2,000, Solana would need to command a valuation of approximately $1.38 trillion under our assumptions.

Using Bitwise’s base-case valuation multiple of 40 times annual network economic value as an illustrative benchmark, Solana would need to generate approximately $34.5 billion in annual economic value to support that figure.

Even at a more generous 60-times multiple, the requirement would be $23 billion annually.

That is substantially more demanding than simply attracting another wave of cryptocurrency traders.

Based on the network’s economic opportunity, competitive landscape, token supply and institutional research, NewsBTC has developed four conditional valuation scenarios.

These ranges are conditional editorial scenarios, not statistically derived forecasts. Outcomes outside these ranges, including substantially greater losses, are possible.

Solana remains relevant but struggles to turn network adoption into meaningful economic value for SOL. Institutional projects develop more slowly than expected, competitors gain market share, and speculative trading remains an important source of demand.

Solana does not need to fail for this scenario to materialize. It only needs to fall short of the expectations investors have placed on it.

Our central expectation assumes Solana retains its position among the leading smart-contract networks while expanding its role in payments, DeFi and tokenized financial assets.

Under this scenario, the network does not need to dominate global finance. It needs to establish a durable position within it and capture more economic value from the applications it supports.

Solana becomes a major platform for tokenized equities, stablecoin settlements and high-frequency financial applications.

Institutional adoption moves beyond announcements, network revenue expands significantly, and the broader cryptocurrency market benefits from favorable liquidity conditions.

At $1,000, SOL would trade at approximately 13.8 times its November 23 reference price.

This is where the most ambitious institutional predictions become conceivable.

Solana would need to capture a significant share of a much larger on-chain financial economy, scale its infrastructure accordingly, and translate that activity into sustained demand for SOL.

An exceptional cryptocurrency bull market could also temporarily push valuations beyond what underlying economics justify.

We would not consider this the most likely outcome based on today’s evidence.

Rather than following every new price target, long-term SOL investors may benefit from monitoring five developments:

Competition from Ethereum, its scaling ecosystem and specialized financial networks remains a considerable risk.

If Solana’s transaction volumes rise while the economic value captured by the network stagnates, we would have reason to lower our valuation assumptions, regardless of how impressive the adoption statistics look.

The current market offers an interesting contradiction.

Solana’s blockchain has established a meaningful financial ecosystem, yet its token is trading roughly 75% below its historical record. Large futures traders are cautious, while institutional research continues to outline substantial long-term opportunities.

Our $180 to $400 base-case range for 2030 reflects the possibility that Solana can grow without fulfilling every ambitious expectation placed on it.

A move toward $1,000 is conceivable under considerably stronger conditions. At $2,000, however, investors would be betting on Solana becoming one of the world’s most valuable digital financial networks.

The opportunity is there. The evidence that would justify such a valuation is not there yet.

For now, the most interesting question surrounding Solana is not how many transactions it can process, but how much those transactions will eventually be worth to SOL holders.

NewsBTC’s analysis places Solana between $180 and $400 by 2030 under our base-case scenario. Strong institutional adoption and improved network economics could support a bullish range of $600 to $1,000, while weaker growth could leave SOL trading between $40 and $110.

Solana could reach $500 by 2030 if its adoption across payments, DeFi and tokenized financial assets continues to expand. Based on an assumed total supply of 690 million SOL, a $500 price would imply a total-supply valuation of approximately $345 billion.

A $1,000 Solana price is possible under a strong bullish scenario. However, achieving and sustaining that valuation would require substantial institutional adoption, higher network economic value and favorable cryptocurrency market conditions. At $1,000, Solana’s implied total-supply valuation would reach approximately $690 billion.

Standard Chartered was reported to have projected a $2,000 SOL price by 2030 in February 2026. However, our analysis considers this an extreme bullish scenario. Reaching $2,000 would imply a total-supply valuation of approximately $1.38 trillion, requiring extraordinary growth in Solana’s financial ecosystem and demand for SOL.

While mathematically possible, a $10,000 SOL price would imply a valuation of approximately $6.9 trillion based on our 2030 supply assumption. There is currently insufficient economic evidence to support such a valuation within this timeframe.

Solana offers long-term exposure to decentralized finance, stablecoin payments and institutional asset tokenization. However, its investment potential depends on whether growing network adoption translates into sustainable demand for SOL. Competition, token inflation, market volatility and regulatory developments remain significant risks.

Solana could challenge Ethereum in areas such as decentralized trading, payments and financial applications. However, overtaking Ethereum by market capitalization would require substantial growth in Solana’s economic value, institutional demand and developer ecosystem. Higher transaction volumes alone would not guarantee that outcome.

VanEck’s October 2023 research placed SOL at $334.70 in its base case and $3,211.28 in its most optimistic scenario for 2030. Standard Chartered was reported to have projected $2,000 in February 2026, while Bitwise’s November 2026 research estimated a base-case price of $385 and a bullish price of $1,100 for 2031.

Weak spot demand, large-holder selling, leveraged liquidations, network disruptions and deteriorating global liquidity could all contribute to further declines. From a technical perspective, losing the $60 to $65 support region identified in our November 23, 2026 analysis would significantly weaken the recovery outlook.

Using the November 23, 2026 reference price of $72.52, a $1,000 investment would purchase approximately 13.79 SOL.

These hypothetical calculations exclude staking rewards, trading fees and taxes. Actual returns may differ substantially, and investors could lose their entire investment.

This analysis uses CoinGlass and PumpGlass market observations dated November 23, 2026, at 21:31 UTC and 19:22 UTC, respectively. Network metrics are provisional DefiLlama observations dated November 23. Technical analysis uses historical Binance SOLUSDT candles. NewsBTC’s valuation scenarios assume 690 million total SOL in 2030 and are conditional editorial estimates rather than statistical forecasts. Third-party forecasts retain their original publication dates and time horizons. Cryptocurrency investments involve significant risk, including loss of principal.

#5093. US Moves to Recover $1.1 Billion From Binance Hack, Saylor's Strategy Buys 457 BTC, XRP Briefly Reclaims $1 — U.Today Crypto Digest

Monday brought a sharp rebound across crypto markets after Bitcoin's weekend crash toward $55,000.

XRP briefly reclaimed $1 as a short squeeze followed a major Nvidia-related rally, while Strategy continued adding Bitcoin to its treasury despite the market downturn.

Meanwhile, U.S. authorities took action to recover more than $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency linked to the October Binance hack.

The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil forfeiture action on Nov. 23 seeking to recover more than $1.1 billion in USDC allegedly stolen from Binance by North Korean hackers.

The assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government. The latest filing represents another step toward recovering funds following the Oct. 29 attack, which reportedly resulted in more than $6 billion in stolen cryptocurrency.

The DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

U.S. authorities said they had helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in cryptocurrency since the theft. The case highlights the role of cooperation between law enforcement agencies and crypto companies in tracking and recovering stolen digital assets.

Strategy purchased another 457 BTC for approximately $29.6 million, according to a Nov. 23 report based on the company's SEC filing.

The latest acquisition was made at an average price of $64,898 per Bitcoin, bringing Strategy's holdings to approximately 851,305 BTC. The company has spent around $64.23 billion accumulating Bitcoin at an average purchase price of $75,446.

The firm's recent purchase comes as the leading cryptocurrency has been struggling to rebound from the heavy sell-off that recently dragged it to a two-plus-year low.

XRP briefly climbed above $1 on Monday after Nvidia's Jensen Huang returned to his roles as CEO and president, triggering a sharp rally in U.S. technology stocks and broader risk assets.

On Binance's XRP/USDT perpetual contract, the token moved from approximately $0.94 to $1.02 within minutes after 14:00 UTC, before retreating to around $0.984.

CoinGlass data cited by U.Today showed that XRP short liquidations exceeded long liquidations by 578%.

Across the crypto market, 110,663 traders were liquidated for $660.89 million over the past 24 hours, while shorts accounted for $515.94 million of that amount.

The move showed how quickly market sentiment can shift during a volatile rebound, particularly when leveraged traders are positioned against a sudden price increase.

#5090. End of Crypto Trading? How AI Replaces Ones Who Pumped Bitcoin (BTC)

The “pump” trade could be taken to new extremes. While some may still be able to use their influence to promote a token, causing others to pile in, it could now be left up to AI to scour socials/wallet activity for abnormal trading volume, assess momentum rankings, etc. and execute on these opportunities faster than those that may be slower to react.

All things considered, agents may exacerbate many of the existing issues with crypto, from short lived moves/reversals, to dangerous herding and even more pronounced drawdowns.

Automation is not necessarily a new occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.

A February 2026 study from the Journal of Futures Markets found sub-second trading patterns in BTC/ETH perpetual/spot markets exhibiting behavior consistent with algo trading for liquidity, increasing volatility and trading costs with no significant impact on prices.

In August 2026, Binance rolled out Agent OS allowing builders to access exchange trading functionality and data via AI agents.

Coinbase Ventures released a comprehensive breakdown of the crypto agentic stack from data, to agent building tools, to execution/compliance in November. Instead of dictating each trade, users may be able to assign high-level goals (i.e. follow momentum, hedge position, etc.) for agents to implement 24/7.

Automation will likely accelerate across the crypto space. While macro events, ETF inflows/outflows, large holders, etc. will still have an impact on Bitcoin, it’s likely that many more aspects/trades will become automated.

Time will tell how pervasive agentic trading will become, but the era of a small group of traders/influencers/chat rooms able to move the needle via FOMO/hype seems poised to face stiff competition from AI that never sleeps.

AI is not necessarily intelligent. A 2026 study published in the journal Frontiers in Blockchain studied machine-learning strategies using crypto market data and found that many strategies became highly overfit and offered no viable edge for retail traders once realistic trading fees were taken into account.

Also, strategies that performed well on one cryptocurrency did not necessarily perform well on others. Faster processing speeds can’t make bad data good, can’t identify all false narratives and can’t insulate a strategy from sudden shifts in market regimes.

Are institutional investors still relevant? Can they protect themselves? Absolutely.

Institutions are (and will continue to be) an important source of capital, liquidity and price discovery (particularly for Bitcoin). A 2026 study using BTC data from 2012–2025 found that as the market has matured, Bitcoin has seen increased trading volume, decreasing transaction costs and increasing market efficiency.

Wintermute reported that in the first half of 2026 institutional clients accounted for 72% of total spot trading volume on its OTC desk (note: this is Wintermute’s OTC desk and is not representative of the entire market). It’s also worth noting that many institutional investors do employ quantitative strategies and state-of-the-art execution technologies.

While larger investors may have access to better data, faster infrastructure, cross-venue surveillance capabilities and stricter risk management protocols (and can limit their exposure and monitor abnormal order flow), there’s only so much that institutional investors can do to protect themselves.

Institutional investors can’t control a 24/7 global market with liquidity spread across multiple venues and derivatives markets. They also can’t assume that all AIs are created equal/safe (as Binance’s launch of its own AI demonstrated prompt injection risks and limited visibility into external AIs’ trading logic/reasons for trading).

Finally, during times of stress, risk management/contingency protocols (used by many investors) could be a crowded exit for funds that employ similar strategies.

The future is not “AI replaces every trader.” It will likely see continued automation of certain aspects of trading (i.e. execution, short-term alpha hunting, etc.) and a continued shift in the value-add that humans bring to the table (i.e. capital allocation, risk management, original research, granting/trading bots permission to trade, etc.).

While AI/bots may continue to squeeze spreads in normal market conditions, they may exacerbate drawdowns/cascades during times of market stress as strategies compete with one another.

At the end of the day, Bitcoin will still be bought/sold, it’s just a question of who gets to make those decisions.

#5089. Bitcoin Reserves Just Found a New Use on Wall Street, but There’s a Catch

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Bitcoin reserves have found another potential use within the US financial system. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has clarified that regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses can count Bitcoin, Ethereum and qualifying payment stablecoins toward certain financial resource requirements. However, the regulator is not prepared to treat those holdings like cash.

The guidance, issued on November 23, could give regulated trading venues greater flexibility in managing their balance sheets. For Bitcoin investors, however, the more interesting question is whether that flexibility will translate into fresh institutional demand.

The answer is not quite as straightforward as it might seem.

The CFTC’s latest advisory addresses three types of regulated businesses: swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organizations.

These institutions are required to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover at least one year of operating costs. Under the new staff guidance, Bitcoin, Ether and qualifying payment stablecoins may contribute toward those requirements, subject to appropriate valuation discounts.

The announcement follows broader efforts to integrate digital assets into regulated financial infrastructure. NewsBTC previously reported on the CFTC’s guidance concerning tokenized collateral at clearinghouses, another area where traditional financial markets are gradually accommodating blockchain-based assets.

This time, the discussion is not about what traders can post as collateral. It is about the assets that the institutions running those markets can rely on to keep their businesses operating.

For a company that already holds Bitcoin, the clarification could make those holdings more useful from a regulatory standpoint. For businesses considering adding cryptocurrency to their balance sheets, it removes some uncertainty surrounding how those assets would be recognized.

But that recognition comes at a discount!

The CFTC advisory references a minimum 20% valuation haircut for Bitcoin and Ethereum, consistent with earlier staff treatment of proprietary cryptocurrency positions held by futures commission merchants.

Qualifying payment stablecoins receive considerably more favorable treatment, with a referenced haircut of 2%.

An exchange holding $10 million in Bitcoin, for example, would be able to count $8 million toward the relevant financial resource requirement if it applied a 20% haircut and no further deductions were necessary.

The remaining $2 million is not a realized loss. It is a regulatory adjustment intended to account for the risk associated with holding a volatile asset.

Crypto assets that are neither readily marketable nor qualifying payment stablecoins would generally face a 100% haircut, effectively excluding them from the calculation.

Perhaps the most revealing part of the advisory is the regulator’s warning about what it calls wrong-way risk.

A DCM should consider potential wrong-way risk

For a cryptocurrency-focused exchange, that risk is particularly relevant. A prolonged Bitcoin sell-off could put pressure on trading revenues while simultaneously reducing the value of the assets the exchange relies on to support its operations.

The problem is not simply that Bitcoin is volatile. It is that its value could deteriorate at precisely the moment a crypto business finds itself under financial pressure.

A 20% valuation discount provides some protection against that scenario, but it is hardly a guarantee.

Despite allowing digital assets to contribute toward broader operating resources, the CFTC has maintained a separate requirement for cash and highly liquid securities.

Bitcoin, Ethereum and even qualifying payment stablecoins cannot be used to satisfy that particular obligation under the advisory.

Swap execution facilities must maintain qualifying liquid resources sufficient to cover at least three months of projected operating expenses or the cost of winding down their operations, whichever is greater.

For designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organizations, the operating-cost liquidity requirement generally covers at least six months.

The distinction matters because an institution can have substantial assets on its balance sheet without necessarily having the cash available to meet immediate obligations.

It is also worth noting that the guidance does not address whether cryptocurrencies can satisfy the separate financial resources that clearinghouses must maintain to cover clearing-member defaults.

In effect, the CFTC is recognizing Bitcoin as an asset that can contribute to an institution’s financial strength without giving it the same regulatory standing as cash.

That is a more cautious approach than some Bitcoin advocates might have hoped for, but arguably a more sustainable one for integrating cryptocurrency into financial infrastructure.

The bullish interpretation is relatively simple. If regulated financial institutions can derive greater utility from holding Bitcoin, more of them may eventually consider allocating capital to the cryptocurrency.

The expansion of regulated crypto infrastructure has already brought digital assets closer to traditional financial markets. Earlier, NewsBTC reported on Coinbase’s CFTC registration for its USDC-focused derivatives clearinghouse, illustrating how cryptocurrency businesses are increasingly operating within established regulatory frameworks.

The latest advisory gives relevant institutions another reason to evaluate how digital assets fit into their balance sheets.

Still, there is a considerable difference between allowing an institution to hold Bitcoin for regulatory purposes and giving it an economic incentive to buy more.

An exchange that already owns Bitcoin could benefit from the clarification without purchasing a single additional coin. Another might conclude that holding conventional securities remains more efficient, particularly given the valuation discounts and separate liquidity requirements.

Nothing in the advisory requires institutions to acquire Bitcoin, and no purchase commitments were disclosed alongside the announcement.

Investors should therefore resist the temptation to translate this development directly into a bullish price forecast.

The longer-term significance may be greater than the immediate market impact. Every additional recognized use for Bitcoin within regulated financial markets strengthens the case for its utility beyond speculative trading.

However, the November 23 document remains a staff advisory rather than a binding rule adopted by the full Commission. It does not amend existing regulations or create enforceable rights.

The next meaningful development will be evidence that regulated institutions are actually changing their reserve allocations in response.

Until then, Bitcoin has gained another form of regulatory recognition. Whether it gains another source of sustained buying pressure is a different question entirely.

The U.S Department of Justice (DOJ) has taken legal action to recover more than $1.1 billion in cryptos stolen from Binance on 29th October 2026. With this move, the government has now moved beyond simply freezing the stolen funds and is now seeking their legal forfeiture.

According to the DOJ, the stolen funds had already been placed under a restraining order, which was the reason why they were prevented from being transferred or accessed while authorities pursued recovery efforts.

Remarking on the same, Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said,

The Department of Justice has long prioritized victims and their rights, and the commencement of this forfeiture action so soon after the restraint of these same assets reflects our commitment to ensuring that victims remain at the forefront of our work.

Binance suffered a cryptocurrency theft worth more than $6.3 billion, which the U.S authorities linked to North Korean cyber hackers.

Following the attack, the hackers allegedly used sophisticated laundering techniques to move the stolen cryptocurrency across different wallets and potentially convert it.

However, the FBI, U.S Secret Service, and the IRS has worked alongside private-sector companies to track the transactions and identify wallets holding the stolen funds.

As its stands, the U.S. government has frozen and seized nearly $3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from multiple sources since the Binance theft. The latest $1.1 billion forfeiture action is part of this broader recovery effort and does not represent an additional $1.1 billion on top of the nearly $3 billion already recovered or restrained.

If this forfeiture is successful, the action could help return the recovered assets to their rightful owners.

#5087. Bitwise XRP ETF Averages $14 Million in Daily Trading in Year One

The Bitwise XRP ETF traded an average of about $14 million a day over its first year on the market, resulting in over $3.5 billion in total trading volume, according to Bitwise.

In a post on X commemorating the Bitwise XRP ETF's first anniversary, Bitwise said the fund had recorded over $667 million in net inflows and had more than $376 million in assets under management (AUM) since launch.

Bitwise's XRP ETF started trading on Nov. 20, 2025, on NYSE Arca. It trades under the same ticker as the cryptocurrency it holds, XRP.

Investors can use the ETF's shares to track the price of the token through their brokerage accounts. The fund holds the XRP on behalf of investors. At launch, the ETF charged a 0.34% annual management fee. It also offered a fee waiver for the first $500 million in assets for the first month.

The $3.5 billion in trading volume is the total value of purchases and sales of the ETF's shares. This means the same ETF shares could trade repeatedly. If an investor sells their shares to another investor, that transaction increases trading volume. But the total XRP held in the fund doesn't change in that case.

On the other hand, the $667 million in net inflows represents the total dollar value of new shares issued over the past year minus redeemed shares.

AUM represents the total dollar value of a fund's assets at a specific moment. Since the fund's total assets are valued in dollars, AUM can fall below cumulative net inflows if the price of XRP declines, even as investors continue to put money into the fund.

The quarterly report filed by Bitwise with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) shows the impact of investor demand and XRP's price on the fund over the past year.

The net asset value of the fund increased from $299.1 million at the end of June to $614.9 million at the end of September.

Over $315.7 million was added to the fund's net assets during that quarter. Just over half of that $315.7 million came from new share creations.

The fund issued new shares with a total dollar value of $210.7 million. It also redeemed $32.8 million in shares during that quarter. So that left about $178 million in net new creations.

The fund issued 13.75 million shares and redeemed 2.42 million shares.

#5085. Binance Hack: US Moves to Recover $1.1 Billion, but Who Gets the Money?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Nearly four weeks after the Binance hack, US authorities have filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October theft. The money is already subject to restrictions, but the latest court filings reveal a complication: freezing stolen cryptocurrency is considerably easier than returning it.

The complaint, filed on November 23, in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, targets USDC associated with 36 cryptocurrency addresses across 18 blockchains.

Federal investigators attribute the October 29 attack to North Korean hacking groups, including the Lazarus Group. The complaint puts the value of the original theft at approximately $6 billion.

For Binance, the latest legal action represents another opportunity to recover a portion of its losses. For the wider cryptocurrency industry, however, the case raises questions about the authority stablecoin issuers exercise over digital assets and what happens when governments become involved.

The assets targeted by US authorities are not an entirely new discovery.

Earlier this month, NewsBTC reported that Circle had frozen approximately $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the Binance hack, following cooperation with law enforcement.

What has changed is the government’s attempt to establish a legal basis for taking possession of those assets.

According to the court documents, US authorities obtained a temporary restraining order on November 12. Prosecutors subsequently requested that the restrictions remain in place throughout the civil forfeiture proceedings.

Both Binance and Circle consented to the initial restraining order and the requested extension, according to the government’s November 23 application.

The agreement between the companies and federal authorities reduces one immediate obstacle to preserving the funds. It does not, however, resolve the question of their ultimate ownership or distribution.

Civil forfeiture proceedings are directed against property believed to be connected to criminal activity. Interested parties can assert legitimate claims to that property through the legal process.

In this case, prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of the assets to the United States. That is not the same thing as a court ordering their immediate return to Binance.

Perhaps the most interesting disclosure in the complaint concerns Circle itself.

The stablecoin issuer can restrict transfers involving USDC held at particular blockchain addresses. However, that authority does not necessarily give Circle direct control over the wallets holding those tokens.

does not have the technical ability to transfer the Defendant Property from the blocklisted Subject Addresses to the United States

Instead, Circle has agreed to issue an equivalent amount of replacement USDC and transfer those tokens to US authorities upon receiving a forfeiture order from the court.

The proposed arrangement exposes an unusual feature of centralized stablecoins. An issuer can prevent tokens from circulating without possessing the private keys needed to move them.

It also raises an accounting question that deserves attention. If replacement tokens are issued, what ultimately happens to the original frozen USDC, and how will Circle ensure that the treatment of those balances is reflected accurately in its outstanding supply and reserve reporting?

The issuance of replacement tokens would not, by itself, prove that USDC had become undercollateralized. Nevertheless, transparency around the implementation would be important for a stablecoin whose credibility depends on confidence in its backing.

The immediate concern is not whether Circle can create new tokens. It is whether the entire recovery process can be independently accounted for.

The temptation to describe the Justice Department’s announcement as a billion-dollar recovery is understandable. It is also premature.

There are three separate stages involved: restricting access to the stolen assets, obtaining legal authority over them and determining how they will ultimately be distributed.

The November 23 filings advance the second stage. They do not establish that the third has been completed.

There is also a cross-border complication.

On November 18, Reuters reported that an Abu Dhabi court had directed several cryptocurrency companies, including Circle, to preserve digital assets associated with the Binance theft.

The involvement of authorities in both the United States and the United Arab Emirates illustrates how a single cryptocurrency theft can generate legal proceedings across multiple jurisdictions.

Blockchain transactions may cross national borders without much difficulty. Establishing ownership rights over the assets involved is a considerably less straightforward exercise.

That does not mean the US and UAE proceedings are necessarily in conflict. But the ultimate disposition of the funds will require more than an announcement from either government.

For investors assessing Binance’s financial position, the distinction between frozen assets and recovered capital is particularly important. Restricted cryptocurrency should not automatically be treated as money already returned to the exchange.

For years, the ability of stablecoin issuers to freeze tokens has been criticized by advocates of decentralized finance.

The Binance case demonstrates the other side of that argument.

Without Circle’s ability to restrict transactions, preserving such a large amount of cryptocurrency for potential recovery would have been more difficult.

In this particular case, centralized control has provided a mechanism that may help prevent suspected criminals from benefiting from stolen assets.

The uncomfortable question is whether the cryptocurrency industry can benefit from that authority while also demanding meaningful safeguards against its misuse.

The answer depends partly on transparency. Token holders should be able to understand why assets were frozen, under what legal authority restrictions remain in place and how disputes over ownership are resolved.

The same standard should apply to the exchange, the stablecoin issuer and the government.

The next significant development in the Binance case will be the court’s treatment of the forfeiture claim and any competing claims to the assets. Circle’s proposed issuance of replacement USDC will also deserve scrutiny if it proceeds.

Until then, the $1.1 billion should be understood as assets subject to an ongoing recovery effort, not a completed repayment.

For a cryptocurrency industry that frequently celebrates the speed of moving money, the Binance hack is a reminder that getting it back can be an entirely different business.

The company is buying back stock using funds previously authorized for repurchases. He didn't specify the number of COIN shares, the price or the amount spent.

At the start of the quarter, Coinbase had $1.96 billion left to repurchase stock. Over the prior three months, it repurchased 37,995 shares for a total cost of $5.3 million, at an average price of $139.91. All repurchases occurred in August, according to its third-quarter report.

Coinbase's board of directors initially authorized stock buybacks of up to $1 billion in October 2024. A year later, the buyback authorization was doubled. The company also received an option to repurchase some outstanding debt.

The board increased the buyback limit again in January 2026, bringing the total authorization to $4 billion.

Some buybacks have been carried out to cancel stock issued as employee compensation. By the end of September, the company had repurchased 10.2 million Class A shares and canceled more than 85% of the stock issued for employee compensation since the fourth quarter of 2024. This is according to an earnings presentation.

Armstrong envisions a scenario where crypto and AI are involved in different aspects of the same transaction.

For example, AI agents might help users make financial decisions and follow their instructions. Then, a crypto network may be used to transfer funds.

Coinbase wants to provide accounts, payment services, and marketplaces for humans and AI agents to use.

"With AI, everybody has a private banker in your pocket that can help you make better financial decisions," Armstrong posted on Nov. 25.

Coinbase added its wallet and payment services to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments. This offers a way for developers to build agents on Amazon and allow the software to discover paid services. Agents can make small payments when necessary.

Now Armstrong is inviting developers to add their specialized AI models to Agentic.Market.

According to Armstrong, an AI agent can choose which specialist to hire for a task based on its capabilities and price. Coinbase provides the platform where agents can find specialists and pay them.

Until USDT’s market cap bottoms, a sustained crypto market bottom may remain out of reach.

DeFi TVL has nearly halved to $70 billion, while the broader crypto market is down over 28% in Q4.

USDT’s shrinking market cap points to continued liquidity outflows, making its recovery a key signal to watch for a market bottom.

#5081. XRP Ledger Bug That Makes Trading Orders Disappear Is Addressed

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Official XRP Ledger's repository account received a proposed fix to keep only transaction-independent offer removals after a tec that should address the disappearance of failed transactions.

This particular change addresses a bug with order-book behavior around “tec” failures, which are failures where the transaction processing is rolled back. In some circumstances, offers can be removed when a "tec" failure occurs, even though the transaction that triggered it never succeeded.

In one scenario, a trader could have an existing offer removed before they’re able to add a replacement (for instance, if they don’t have enough reserve to add a new offer). In another, a more complicated Flow could temporarily leave an offer unfunded, only to have funds restored if a subsequent step fails, again resulting in an offer being removed even though the transaction that triggered it failed.

To address this issue, rippled will attempt to remove offers that were marked for removal upon tec failure any time a tec failure occurs. Previously, this was attempted for certain tec error codes but not others, with some additional restrictions around Flow-related offer removals (an offer will only be marked for removal if the owner’s balance has not changed in any relevant ways during the course of the Flow).

Offers that have already expired can still be removed, but offers owned by the transactor will be skipped. This is a best effort to make sure offers are consistently added/removed from the order book and should reduce confusing trade results.

Offers to/from regular XRP accounts and balances, XRP sends are unaffected and there are no proposed API changes.

This does not change XRP supply, fees, transaction capacity, etc. and is unlikely to have any effect on XRPL usage or XRP price (other than maybe making XRPL trading more appealing to traders).

This change would mostly affect traders using decentralized exchanges (DEXs) and particularly those using complex/routed/fill-or-kill orders/self-crosses.

On November 23, XRP briefly hit $1.026 before dropping below $1. Reports indicate crypto selling in general and ETF outflows have been putting pressure on XRP lately. By November 25, XRP was trading at ~$0.92. This software change would not be a catalyst for a price recovery of XRP.

BitMine, the world’s largest Ethereum [ETH] DAT, has reportedly reached investments (including crypto) worth $11.1 billion as of 23rd November.

Meanwhile, the company has staked 5.22 million ETH, representing approximately 86% of its holdings. BitMine estimates that its current staked holdings could generate $245 million in annualized revenue, potentially rising to $286 million once all its ETH is staked.

At the same time, SharpLink repurchased $10 million worth of its own shares (SBET), signalling its confidence in the company’s long-term strategy and its current valuation.

For SharpLink, the move is also linked to its Ethereum treasury strategy. The company aims to increase its ETH per share, which measures how much Ethereum backs each outstanding company share.

By reducing the number of shares in circulation through buybacks, SharpLink can potentially increase this metric without purchasing additional ETH.

These accumulation strategies coincided with ETH’s price trading at $1,692.78 following a drop of 1.9% at press time.

Despite a drop below the $2K price level, however, crypto analyst Michaël van de Poppe pointed out that Ethereum’s performance against Bitcoin has remained relatively stable. In fact, over the past two weeks, Bitcoin saw a sharp 25% decline.

That’s a sign of strength, as generally, markets would be absolutely collapsing when it comes to altcoins vs. Bitcoin.

This is noteworthy because altcoins typically suffer heavier losses than Bitcoin during market downturns as investors move towards relatively safer assets. ETH’s ability to hold its ground against BTC could therefore indicate improving relative strength and potentially growing investor interest.

Van de Poppe also claimed that Ethereum may be approaching a possible trend reversal. For this to happen, the ETH/BTC trading pair needs to break above the 0.0290 level and reclaim its 21-day moving average.

Echoing similar sentiments, another analyst noted that Bitcoin has been trading within a nine-month range and recently recorded a lower low, raising concerns about further downside.

Ethereum, meanwhile, recovered from its June bottom, rallied by approximately 86%, and subsequently held above its previous low of $1,506. This might allude to a potential higher-low formation for ETH, hinting at an improving market structure.

All in all, Bitcoin is still struggling to establish a convincing bottom, while Ethereum has been showing signs of relative strength. However, ETH needs to break key resistance levels before a sustained uptrend can be confirmed.

Here, it’s worth noting that Ethereum’s Taker Buy/Sell Ratio has remained largely below 1 throughout November 2026, indicating that aggressive selling volume exceeded aggressive buying volume across exchanges. At press time, the ratio stood at 0.98, hinting at sustained selling pressure and relatively weak buying demand.

Additionally, CoinShares recently sold its entire Ethereum holdings in October, generating $19.3 million. Given that it will use these millions to repurchase its own shares under a $40 million buyback program, caution makes sense.

#5078. Bitcoin Loses $60,000 And Gold Offers No Protection During Its Worst Selloff Since 1982

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

The Bitcoin price fell back below $60,000 on Tuesday, cutting short a recovery that had taken the cryptocurrency above $64,000 a day earlier. But perhaps the more troubling development for investors is happening outside the crypto market.

Gold is going through a severe correction of its own, leaving investors in two assets often associated with wealth preservation facing substantial losses.

This is not the first time Bitcoin and gold have struggled simultaneously. What makes the current environment particularly difficult is that neither asset generates income at a time when interest-bearing investments offer an increasingly attractive alternative.

The question is no longer simply whether Bitcoin is digital gold. It is whether investors have enough reason to own either asset under current monetary conditions.

The selling extended well beyond Bitcoin. Figures from the World Gold Council show that Bitcoin lost 13.7%, gold fell 8.3% and the Nasdaq dropped 10%, while the US Dollar Index gained 0.4%. The numbers point to a broader reduction in risk exposure rather than a selloff specific to crypto.

Gold declined 24.6% over the 60 days ending November 23, its steepest loss over such a period since 1982.

The World Gold Council’s latest market assessment, published on Monday, identified several risks facing the precious metal, including pressure on leveraged equity and credit positions, restrictive monetary policy and the possibility of another disappointing US inflation report.

The organization also identified the lack of a clear reduction in speculative positioning as a concern.

This matters for Bitcoin because the argument for buying BTC during a gold correction often assumes that capital leaving one scarce asset will eventually find its way into the other.

There is little reason to assume that happens automatically.

An investor selling gold to reduce leverage or meet a margin requirement is unlikely to replace that exposure immediately with Bitcoin. The priority is raising cash, not finding another store of value.

There is also a difference between selling an asset because its investment thesis has deteriorated and selling because the cost of maintaining a position has become too expensive. The latter can create opportunities for patient buyers, but it rarely provides a reliable indication of when a market will bottom.

Monday’s trading session offered Bitcoin investors some encouragement. The cryptocurrency recovered above $64,000 following the previous week’s decline to its lowest levels in roughly two years.

The broader picture is hardly encouraging. Bitcoin has lost nearly 24% over the past three months, falling from a period high of $86,578 to a low of $58,178. Although BTC has since recovered above $60,000, the bounce has done little to change the broader downward trend.

Tuesday’s return below $60,000 raises questions about the strength of the recovery, particularly given the improvement in technology stocks during Monday’s session.

If Bitcoin struggles to sustain gains when conditions improve elsewhere, investors should be careful about assuming that another equity market rally will necessarily pull BTC higher.

There is also an important distinction between a recovery driven by fresh buyers and one driven by traders closing profitable short positions. Both can produce impressive green candles. Only the former demonstrates that investors are willing to commit new capital at higher prices.

Spot trading activity, ETF subscriptions and derivatives positioning will offer a better indication of which type of recovery the market is experiencing.

For now, the failure to retain Monday’s gains makes the rebound less convincing than its initial size suggested.

Bitcoin’s recent performance will inevitably revive criticism of its role as a store of value. However, gold’s own losses make that argument considerably less straightforward.

The metal has been used to preserve wealth for centuries, yet it remains vulnerable to changes in interest rates, investor positioning and the strength of the US dollar.

Bitcoin shares some of those vulnerabilities while carrying considerably different market risks, including its dependence on speculative demand and the availability of leverage across cryptocurrency exchanges.

That does not invalidate Bitcoin’s scarcity argument. Its supply characteristics have not changed because its market price has fallen.

What the current correction does challenge is the assumption that scarcity alone guarantees protection during financial stress.

An asset can have a credible long-term investment case and still be a poor short-term hedge. Bitcoin investors would benefit from separating those two propositions rather than defending both every time the market declines.

The immediate focus now turns to Wednesday’s US inflation release.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis is scheduled to publish its October personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report on November 25. The previous release showed annual headline PCE inflation of 3.6%, with core inflation at 3.1%.

Another stronger-than-expected reading could reinforce expectations of restrictive monetary policy, making conditions more difficult for assets that rely heavily on capital appreciation.

A softer reading, particularly if accompanied by falling Treasury yields, could offer some relief to both Bitcoin and gold.

For Bitcoin, however, recovering $60,000 should be treated as a starting point rather than confirmation of a broader reversal. Monday’s trading high above $64,000 represents a more demanding test of whether buyers are prepared to return.

Until that happens, the market has demonstrated that it can bounce. It has yet to demonstrate that it can sustain a recovery.

#5077. Dogecoin Creator Explains Why No One Can Predict Crypto Prices

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Dogecoin co-founder Billy Markus, who is known on X as Shibetoshi Nakamoto, has explained why, in his opinion, no one can predict the prices of cryptocurrencies.

Markus shared his opinion on Wednesday in a reply to an X post with a prediction that the price of Zcash (ZEC) would fall to $100.

"my opinion is that every single cryptocurrency has an arbitrary value mostly unrelated to anything except that people believe they can make more money if others buy it from them in the future and thus all future projections are pissing in the wind," the Dogecoin co-founder wrote.

Markus did not mention Zcash or any other token by name in his reply, and his post was about every single cryptocurrency on the market, including the one he created himself.

my opinion is that every single cryptocurrency has an arbitrary value mostly unrelated to anything except people believe they can make more money if others buy it from them in the future and thus all future projections are pissing in the wind

At the time of the post, ZEC was trading at around $728, up by 41.3% over the past year, according to price data on X.

The latest comment from Markus comes a week after Bitwise filed an S-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a spot Zcash ETF. According to the filing, the fund is set to trade on the Texas Stock Exchange under the ticker ZEC, and it will not stake ZEC or use shielded transactions.

Markus created Dogecoin together with Jackson Palmer in December 2013. The two developers based the cryptocurrency on the Doge meme with a Shiba Inu dog, and they launched it as a joke about the crypto market of that time.

Markus has said in the past that it took him a couple of hours to write the code of Dogecoin. In 2021, Markus also said on X that he had sold all of his DOGE in 2015 after he lost his job, and that he got about the price of a used Honda Civic for it.

Since then, Markus has stayed active on X under the Shibetoshi Nakamoto name, and he often replies to posts about crypto prices, forecasts and new tokens.

In June 2022, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates spoke about crypto and NFTs at the TechCrunch Sessions: Climate conference.

"As an asset class, it's 100% based on the greater fool theory — that somebody's going to pay more for it than I do," Gates said.

Earlier, at the Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting in April 2022, Warren Buffett said that he would not buy all of the Bitcoin in the world even for $25.

"If you told me you own all of the bitcoin in the world and you offered it to me for $25, I wouldn't take it because what would I do with it?" Buffett said.

According to Buffett, Bitcoin does not produce anything. At the same meeting, Buffett compared it with farmland and apartment buildings, and he said that he would pay for a share of them because farmland produces food and apartments produce rent.

#5076. Bitcoin ETFs gained 191 institutional holders but just 25 drove all the growth

The largest investment managers added nearly 57,000 BTC-equivalent in the third quarter as the rest collectively reduced their exposure.

More investment managers reported holding US spot Bitcoin products in the third quarter, but the growth in their positions came from a much smaller group.

Galaxy Research found that the 25 largest holders at Sept. 30 added more Bitcoin exposure than all reporting managers combined. Everyone outside that group, taken together, cut exposure.

Galaxy's Nov. 19 analysis of Form 13F filings counted 2,166 investment managers with positions as of Sept. 30, up 191 from June. Their disclosed holdings reached nearly $29.8 billion, or the equivalent of 356,491 BTC, across 13 US spot products, including an over-the-counter trust.

The Bitcoin-equivalent figure translates fund shares into their underlying Bitcoin exposure.

The filings describe a quarter that ended weeks before US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded roughly $2.4 billion in net outflows over five trading sessions through Nov. 23.

The 25 largest managers at the end of September held 60.8% of the disclosed exposure in Galaxy's dataset, and added a net 56,922 BTC-equivalent over the quarter.

The rest of the reporting managers reduced their holdings by 7,693 BTC-equivalent combined, leaving an overall net addition of 49,229.

Galaxy ranks the group by holdings on Sept. 30 and converts the change in reported shares into BTC-equivalent at September-end rates. A rising Bitcoin price alone cannot account for the increase.

The 25 largest filers added more than the total net increase, while other managers trimmed their exposure.

The top 25 held 60.8% of disclosed exposure and accounted for the whole net increase.

Form 13F captures reportable long share positions. The comparison covers disclosed holdings in Galaxy’s 13-product sample, including one OTC trust, and cannot identify underlying clients or offsetting positions.

Galaxy ranked filers by Sept. 30, 2026 positions across 13 U.S. spot Bitcoin products. The top 25 held 60.8%. The remainder is 100% minus 60.8%, or 39.2%. The change for other filers is 49,229 minus 56,922, or −7,693 BTC-equivalent. Change bars use the same zero and unit.

Form 13F captures reportable long share positions. The comparison covers disclosed holdings in Galaxy’s 13-product sample, including one OTC trust, and cannot identify underlying clients or offsetting positions.

Widening the group to the 50 largest holders makes the offset clearer. They added 59,578 BTC-equivalent, while everyone else cut 10,349.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Wells Fargo led the additions at 14,636 BTC-equivalent, followed by Brevan Howard at 8,606, Bank of America at 7,201, Millennium Management at 7,114, and Jane Street at 6,180.

Wells Fargo finished September with 30,553 BTC-equivalent in reported exposure, moving ahead of Jane Street, which ended the quarter at 23,167.

Galaxy counted 358 managers that disclosed positions after reporting none in June, while 167 dropped out. The newcomers had a combined 9,554 BTC-equivalent, just 2.7% of the reported holdings at quarter-end.

Separately, Bloomberg senior ETF analyst James Seyffart reported on Nov. 24 that more than 2,200 institutions held Bitcoin ETFs and said investment advisers dominated known ownership in his analysis.

A manager with a small newly disclosed position counts just as much toward participation as a large platform taking a much bigger position. And an existing holder can add a position worth far more than those newcomers put together without changing the headcount.

More managers can bring a wider set of investors into the funds while leaving the net increase sensitive to changes in a few large positions.

Across the 12 exchange-listed products Galaxy tracked, 13F filers accounted for 27.6% of the Bitcoin in the funds at Sept. 30.

The 10 largest filers held 41.9% of that disclosed exposure. A handful of financial groups can dominate the positions visible in those filings, while most of the funds’ Bitcoin backs shares held outside the 13F tally.

Galaxy’s breakdown traced 26,016 BTC-equivalent to Wells Fargo’s adviser and brokerage arms at the end of September, up from 13,219 in June.

The increase at Bank of America came mainly from its dealer and trading units, whose reported positions reached 7,626 BTC-equivalent, up from 421 in June.

Brokerage positions can include assets managed for clients, while trading positions can include inventory or one side of a hedge. SEC guidance on Form 13F requires managers to report eligible positions over which they exercise investment discretion and to leave short positions out.

A filing can show a sizable long position even if a trade elsewhere offsets some of its sensitivity to Bitcoin's price. It also gives little visibility into how many underlying investors sit behind a brokerage unit's reported position.

Across the 12 listed products, Galaxy put advisers and wealth platforms at 40.5% of reported September holdings. That category includes broker-dealer platforms, whose dealer and trading desks can also contribute to the totals.

The category added about half of the net increase in that product set.

The September quarter ended with Bitcoin at $83,580, according to Galaxy. By Nov. 16 it was $64,943, and the funds Galaxy tracked held 38,531 fewer BTC than at quarter-end.

The daily US spot Bitcoin ETF figures from Farside Investors then showed five consecutive sessions of net withdrawals from Nov. 17 through Nov. 23. Withdrawals reached $669.2 million on Nov. 20 and $569.7 million on Nov. 23.

Daily net flows in USD millions. Dates show November 2026 trading sessions.

Source: Farside Investors, daily U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF flows

An ETF can see withdrawals while some holders retain or add to their positions, as the largest holders increased their exposure in the third quarter while other filers cut theirs overall.

The next set of filings can show which September positions were still reported at December’s quarter-end and whether managers outside September’s top 25 increased their combined exposure.

The headcount measures participation among filers, while the distribution of changes shows whether the increase in reported fund-share exposure is spreading across more of those managers.
